    visualize where each respondent's lat/long fall into one of the 10km grid polygons.

3.  Use `st_join()` to do the same "layering" process behind the scenes. `st_join()` takes
    each respondent's point geometry, places it into a 10km polygon, and extracts the
    corresponding 10km grid polygon's attribute data into the survey data. This will
    assign the 10km grid identification number to every respondent, which we will then use
    in a tabular merge to integrate the smoke data.

4.  Finally, perform a `left_join()` based on the 10km grid ID variable and survey date
    variable to integrate the tabular smoke_10km data into the survey data.

```{r, use_case_3_spatialjoin, echo=TRUE}
# -- Make Survey Data Spatial using lat/long variables ----
# convert to sf_points object
  survey_points <- st_as_sf(survey_df,
                            coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
                            crs = master_crs) 
  
# -- map survey_points over 10km_grid to visualize st_join() procedure ----
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = sf_wi_10km,
            color = "gray80") +
    geom_sf(data = survey_points,
            color = "red",
            size = 0.30) 

# -- Place point in a 10km grid and extract grid polygon attributes ----
# spatial join attributes from grid geometry into survey data rows
  survey_points <- st_join(survey_points, sf_wi_10km) |> 
    dplyr::select(-COORDY) |> 
    dplyr::select(-COORDX)

# -- Tabular join smoke data based on survey date and 10km grid id ----
# rename columns to match survey_points dataframe
  temp <- smoke_10km |> 
    rename(ID = grid_id_10km,
           survey_date = date)

# left_join smoke data to survey data
  survey_10km <- left_join(survey_points,
                           temp,
                           by = c("ID", "survey_date"))

# clean up environment
  rm(temp, survey_points)
```

Now, we have basic smoke data for each respondent, matching the date they took each survey
wave. We integrated data at three different levels: the county, tract, and 10km grid. The
data is stored in three separate data frames, one for each level of geography
(`survey_10km`, `survey_county`, and `survey_tract`).

Investigate the data.frames using the `View(survey_10km)` function typed directly into the
console.

## Use Case #4: Spatial Buffer and Spatial Interpolation

Use case \# 3 assigned county, tract, and 10km grid smoke data to each survey respondent
record. The assignment was based on the precise lat/long of each respondents home address.
Let's map a selection of these points over county and 10km grids to visualize the which
county data and 10km grid data are assigned to each respondent.

```{r, use_case_4_map1, echo=TRUE}
# convert to sf_points object
  survey_points <- st_as_sf(survey_df,
                            coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
                            crs = master_crs)
  
# see extent of survey_buffer object for mapping purposes
  st_bbox(survey_points)

# map for sanity check
  ggplot() + 
    # grid layer
    geom_sf(data = sf_wi_10km,
            color = "gray80",
            fill = NA) +
    # county boundary layer
    geom_sf(data = sf_county_2010,
            color = "black",
            fill = NA) +
    # point layer
    geom_sf(data = survey_points,
            color = "red",
            size = 0.5) +
    # restrict plot to just lat/longs in northwest, based of of st_bbox() output
    coord_sf(xlim = c(-92.86145, -89), 
             ylim = c(45.5, 46.81861)) +
    # labels
    labs(title = "Respondent address location",
         subtitle = "placed in county and 10km grid context") +
    theme_void()
```

Note that some points fall along county borders. Perhaps the county average is not an
appropriate measure of smoke exposure. What if a respondent lives in the very corner of a
large county, and does most of their daily living across the county border?

Or, what if they live at the very corner of a 10km grid? Is the smoke exposure value for
that single 10km grid the best measure for that respondent? In both cases, wouldn't we
want some information about the grids or counties nearby?

To address this, we can generate distance buffers around point geometries and use spatial
data operations to gather the smoke data from the areas within the buffers. This is
opposed to relying on nominally assigned aggregated data, like counties or 10km polygons.
This process is called spatial interpolation. It is useful when standard geographies are
not quite appropriate for your exposure measure.

Let's perform a spatial interpolation step by step, and through the process highlight some
examples for why this is a useful procedure.

### Generate buffer polygons around point data

First, we will convert the point data to a custom distance buffer polygon. Examine the
shapefile's CRS to see which units the projection uses.

```{r, use_case_4_crsunits, echo=TRUE}
# check for units in survey_points crs
  st_crs(survey_points)
```

In our case, the CRS uses meters (LENGTHUNIT["metre",1]). Let's generate a buffer of 20km
diameter around each point, and map them over the 10km grid and the county boundaries.

```{r, use_case_4_buffermap, echo=TRUE}
# -- Make buffer polygon ----
# 10km radus, 20km diameter
  survey_buffer <- st_buffer(survey_points, dist = 10000) 
  
# map for sanity check
  ggplot() + 
  # grid layer
    geom_sf(data = sf_wi_10km,
            color = "gray80",
            fill = NA) +
  # county boundary layer
    geom_sf(data = sf_county_2010,
            color = "black",
            fill = NA) +
  # buffer layer
    geom_sf(data = survey_buffer,
            color = "red",
            fill = "red",
            alpha = 0.1) +
  # point layer
    geom_sf(data = survey_points,
            color = "red",
            size = 0.3) +
  # zoom to just a few counties in northwest
    coord_sf(xlim = c(-92.86145, -89), 
             ylim = c(45.5, 46.81861)) +
  # labels
    labs(title = "Respondent address buffer",
         subtitle = "20km radius") +
    theme_void()
```

### Interpolate smoke data for each buffer

We will use `st_interpolate_aw()` to calculate smoke values based on the 10km grids that
fall within the buffer polygon, ***NOT*** based just on the single 10km grid that the
lat/long falls within. `st_interpolate_aw()` performs and area-weighted interpolation of
underlying polygon data. This means that the area of each underlying polygon that you are
extracting data from serves as the weight when when calculating the average of the
underlying polygon data. A grid that is only 1% covered by the 20km buffer contributes an
appropriately sized share to the average.

Because we need to repeat this procedure for many different dates, we will perform the
interpolation in a `for` loop, executing the `st_interpolate_aw()` day by day. This
process will take a few minutes becasue we are inefficiently performing many spatial
interpolation procedures over and over. This procedure will produce accurate results, but
showcases the limits of vector based data integration procedures over many cases,
variables, or with timeseries data.

Let's define the for loop parameters:

1.  Define an empty list object to store interpolated data from each loop iteration.

2.  Define a list of the dates in the survey data that we need to access in the smoke_10km
    data.frame.

3.  Define the smoke_10km variables we want to extract

```{r, use_case_4_forloopparamerters, echo=TRUE}
# -- For Loop parameters ----
# empty list object
  survey_list <- list()

# list of dates in survey data
  survey_dates <- survey_df |> 
    dplyr::select(survey_date) |> 
    group_by(survey_date) |> 
    slice(1) |> 
    ungroup()
  
  survey_dates <- c(survey_dates$survey_date)

# for testing, use below survey_dates with few dates
# replace 3 with some number to sample smaller N of dates
  # survey_dates <- sample(survey_dates$survey_date, 3, replace = FALSE)

# list of variables to merge
  smoke_vars <- c("smokePM_pred",
                  "mean_30day",
                  "mean_7day")
```

Then, run the loop. The loop performs the following processes for each date in the survey
data:

1.  Reduce the survey data and the smoke_10km data to a single date.

2.  Use `right_join()` with tabular `smoke_10km` and shapefile `sf_wi_10km` to spatialize
    the smoke data.

3.  Perform a spatial interpolation on the smoke variables.

4.  Append the interpolated averages back to the tabular survey_buffer data.

5.  Save that date's data to a list.

```{r, use_case_4_forloop, echo=TRUE}
# -- For loop to perform spatial interopolation ----
# for every date in the survey...
  for (d_i in survey_dates) {
  # make temporary naming object
    date_name <- c(d_i)
    
  # filter the survey_buffer data to a single date, d_i
    survey_temp <- survey_buffer |> 
      filter(survey_date == d_i)
    
  # skip to next date if no records exist in survey_temp
  # (this is a sanity check. Our survey_dates list of dates is defined 
  # from the actual data source, so there should not be iteration that 
  # does not have data.)
    if (nrow(survey_temp) == 0) next
    
  # filter smoke_10km data to single date, d_i
    smoke_temp <- smoke_10km |> 
      filter(date == d_i) |> 
      rename(ID = grid_id_10km)
    
  # make smoke_temp spatial
    smoke_temp <- right_join(sf_wi_10km, smoke_temp, by = "ID") |> 
      dplyr::select(smoke_vars)
    
  # use_st_interpolate_aw() function
    temp <- st_interpolate_aw(smoke_temp, survey_temp, extensive = FALSE)
    
  # append interpolated columns to survey_temp
    survey_temp$pm25_w_avg <- temp$smokePM_pred
    survey_temp$mean_30day_w_avg <- temp$mean_30day
    survey_temp$mean_7day_w_avg <- temp$mean_7day
    
  # append to list
    survey_list[[paste0(d_i,"weighted_avg")]] <- survey_temp
    
  # clean up
    rm(survey_temp,
       temp,
       smoke_temp)
    
  } # close for loop

  gc()
```

Finally, let's stack the list objects for each individual date back into a standard
dataframe. Use `View()` to examine the `survey_buffer` data and newly created
`pm25_w_avg`, `mean_30day_w_avg`, and `mean_7day_w_avg` variables.

```{r, use_case_4_stack, echo=TRUE}
# stack interpolated dataframe
survey_buffer <- bind_rows(survey_list)
```

## Compare different levels of data integration

Let's make a final data set, `survey_final`, that has the county level, tract level, 10km
grid level, and interpolated buffer level measures of smoke data.

```{r, ecombine_and_compare, echo=TRUE}
# -- Compare Point-level differences ----
# ---- Combine all smokePM_pred values into one df ----

# make our final survey data set
  survey_final <- as.data.frame(survey_buffer)

# append 10km_grid level to final
  temp <- as.data.frame(survey_10km) |>  
    dplyr::select(respondent_ID, ID, survey_wave, smoke_vars) |> 
    rename(grid_id = ID,
           pm25_grid = smokePM_pred,
           mean_30day_grid = mean_30day,
           mean_7day_grid = mean_7day)
  
  survey_final <- left_join(survey_final, temp, by = c("respondent_ID", "survey_wave"))

# traappend tract level to final
  temp <- as.data.frame(survey_tract) |>  
    dplyr::select(respondent_ID, survey_wave, smoke_vars) |> 
    rename(pm25_tract = smokePM_pred,
           mean_30day_tract = mean_30day,
           mean_7day_tract = mean_7day)
  
  survey_final <- left_join(survey_final, temp, by = c("respondent_ID", "survey_wave"))

# append county level to final
  temp <- as.data.frame(survey_county) |> 
    dplyr::select(respondent_ID, survey_wave, smoke_vars) |> 
    rename(pm25_county = smokePM_pred,
           mean_30day_county = mean_30day,
           mean_7day_county = mean_7day)
  
  survey_final <- left_join(survey_final, temp, by = c("respondent_ID", "survey_wave"))
```

Now, we have a single data frame where, for each respondent, we have measures of smoke
exposure captured at county, tract, 10km grid, and the 10km weighted average based on the
20km point buffer. Perform any comparisons or robustness checks using these variables the
same way you might in any tabular data set. Additionally, because the data is spatial, you
can account for spatial relationships in your analyses using spatial regression
techniques.

# Concluding Remarks -

The above case studies demonstrate typical ways to integrate gridded, vector-based
high-frequency spatio-temporal data with population and survey data. They demonstrate the
process using both standardized geographic boundaries and identifiers (county and tract
FIPS) as well as non-standard geographic identifiers (10km grids).

Gridded environmental data is an accessible, low-demand way to integrate environmental
data into social science, population, and health research. The above workflow may vary
from data set to data set, but is largely applicable to vector-based gridded data.

Finally, note that vector-based gridded data is not typically generated at the finest
level of spatial and temporal specificity. If you require environmental data that is
specific to the hour, specific to a small area (meters, not miles), or expansive over very
wide ranges and time frames, then raster-based environmental data may be necessary.
Processing raster-based data requires additional R packages, more computing power
including parallel processing, and data storage solutions. See the resources in Part 1:
Raster Data, and the below resources. Many entries have guidance on processing
raster-based environmental data.
